title: Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets
coreMove: Place each clarified commitment into the bucket where it can be trusted and acted on: calendar, next actions, waiting-for, projects, reference, or someday-maybe.

exampleSpecs.domain: an emergency department charge nurse sorting post-shift administrative commitments
exampleSpecs.audience: a nurse supervisor who leaves work with scraps of reminders in three pockets
exampleSpecs.stakes: a certification deadline, a supply request, and a staffing follow-up could all blur into one anxious pile
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the nurse separates the hard calendar deadline from next physical actions, waiting-for items, and reference notes instead of keeping one overloaded task list

exampleSpecs.domain: a youth soccer coach handling parent texts, field permits, and uniform orders
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer coach with a day job and twenty families expecting clear answers
exampleSpecs.stakes: practice space, child safety forms, and game-day readiness depend on reminders not vanishing in text threads
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the coach says out loud where each reminder belongs, including putting the parks department reply on a waiting-for list rather than repeatedly worrying about it

exampleSpecs.domain: a probate attorney organizing estate documents after a client meeting
exampleSpecs.audience: a small-practice lawyer who handles deadlines, client communication, and document storage without much support staff
exampleSpecs.stakes: a filing date could be missed if legal reference material, client follow-up, and court deadlines sit in the same folder
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the attorney distinguishes reference documents from calendar commitments and writes the next action as a visible physical step, not as the vague label 'estate case'

exampleSpecs.domain: a restaurant line cook preparing for a surprise health inspection follow-up
exampleSpecs.audience: a kitchen lead who thinks best on the move but loses track of deferred fixes
exampleSpecs.stakes: a small repair, a supplier call, and a cleaning checklist could affect the inspection result and the next service rush
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the cook keeps the project outcome visible while parking separate next actions by context, so the bucket supports service instead of becoming list theater

exampleSpecs.domain: a parent organizing school accommodation paperwork for a ten-year-old
exampleSpecs.audience: a household captain balancing school emails, medical forms, and family logistics
exampleSpecs.stakes: the child may wait longer for support if meeting dates, forms, and replies from specialists are not held in reliable places
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the parent notices that caring more is not enough and creates separate buckets for the calendar meeting, the next form to complete, the specialist reply being waited on, and reference records

exampleSpecs.domain: a freelance saxophonist coordinating a three-city weekend tour
exampleSpecs.audience: a working musician managing travel, venue contacts, set lists, and invoices between rehearsals
exampleSpecs.stakes: one lost confirmation or unpaid invoice could turn a profitable tour into a scramble
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the musician traces a past failure to keeping confirmations buried in email, then reorganizes travel details as reference, venue replies as waiting-for, and outreach as context-based next actions

exampleSpecs.domain: a volunteer disaster relief coordinator triaging supply requests after a flood
exampleSpecs.audience: a community organizer receiving urgent requests from shelters, donors, and drivers
exampleSpecs.stakes: scarce supplies may go to the wrong place if every request is treated as equally immediate
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the coordinator resists making one priority pile and instead assigns each clarified item to calendar, next-action, waiting-for, project support, or reference buckets so urgency does not erase structure
